deck.headline: Anthropic slips below its $83 IPO price as Nvidia gives back Monday's rally
deck.sub: Four sessions after the biggest listing on record, the Claude maker trades under its offer price; Nvidia drops 5.9% and the Nasdaq 1.5% while the Dow climbs back above 50,000.
deck.summary: Anthropic closed at $81.90 on Tuesday, below its $83 IPO price, four sessions after the record listing. Nvidia gave back 5.9% after Monday's 31.5% jump and the Nasdaq fell 1.5%, while the Dow rose above 50,000. Markets price a 98% chance of a Fed rate rise in December.
deck.whyItMatters: An AI IPO priced for a boom is already under water while rate rises are coming; banks with exposure to AI-linked lending, data-centre credit or margin books on these names should expect more volatility, not less, into the 9 Dec Fed decision.
deck.checked: Closing prices checked on Yahoo Finance chart data (opened); market narrative from Reuters via Mint (opened)
deck.storyline: Storyline: AI stocks and market mood · day 5
deck.detailHtml:
Anthropic closed at $81.90 on Tuesday, down 6.5% and below the $83 price of its 19 Nov IPO, which raised about $81bn. The stock opened at $111.50 on its first day and has fallen in every session since. Nvidia gave back 5.9% to $155.38 after Monday's 31.5% surge on Jensen Huang's return. The Nasdaq fell 1.5% to 23,733.54 and the S&P 500 0.5%, while the Dow rose 0.85% to 50,018.70 as money rotated into older industries. Reuters quotes Cetera's Gene Goldman: one headline "doesn't really resolve investor questions about the AI trade". Fed funds futures price a 98% chance of a December rate rise and 66% for another in January; US PCE inflation data is due on Wednesday. Early on Wednesday, Tokyo's Nikkei fell more than 2%, led by chip stocks (WSJ).

Anthropic listed on 19 Nov in the largest IPO on record, pricing at $83 a share. It opened at $111.50 and closed its first day at $97.17, then slid to $88.91, $87.64 and, on Tuesday, $81.90. That is the first close below the offer price.

The fall came as the market cooled after Monday, when Nvidia jumped 31.5% on Jensen Huang's reinstatement. On Tuesday Nvidia lost 5.9%, the Nasdaq 1.5% and the S&P 500 0.5%; the Dow rose 0.85% to just above 50,000. The 10-year Treasury yield was little changed at about 4.93%, Brent crude rose 2.3% to $91.40 on attacks on ships near the Strait of Hormuz, and gold fell 2.7%.

Investors are now waiting for Wednesday's PCE inflation figures, the last major data before the Fed's 8-9 Dec meeting, where a rate rise is almost fully priced.

deck.headline: Hackers breach a CIA and ODNI open-source intelligence system
deck.summary: A CIA and ODNI system for analysing open-source intelligence was breached, the NYT reported and AP and CyberScoop confirmed. Sources say no classified networks were involved and the issue is resolved; what was taken and by whom is unknown. It follows an FBI database hack and an NSA network outage this month.
deck.whyItMatters: The US intelligence community's outward-facing tools are being hit in the same month as bank and cloud outages; banks that share threat data with government channels should assume those feeds can be watched.
deck.checked: Checked on CyberScoop and AP via SecurityWeek (both opened); NYT original not opened; no official statement
deck.storyline: Storyline: hacks on US government systems · day 1
deck.detailHtml: An unclassified system that the CIA and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence use to analyse open-source intelligence (news, commercial satellite images, data-broker feeds) was breached, The New York Times reported on 24 Nov; AP and CyberScoop confirmed it through unnamed sources. A source told CyberScoop the hack "did not involve our classified networks"; AP's source says the issue has been resolved. It is not known what was taken or who did it; the CIA declined to comment. It follows an apparent hack of an FBI national criminal-justice database and a temporary outage of an NSA classified network this month. Huntress's Ben Bernstein notes that seeing what analysts search for reveals US intelligence priorities without touching a classified file.
deck.sourcesHtml: REPORTINGCyberScoop: Unclassified intel system hit by hackers, affecting CIA, ODNI · AP via SecurityWeek: An unclassified CIA system was breached in a cyberattack

deck.headline: Attackers using AI tools broke into Check Point firewall management servers at 22 firms
deck.summary: GreyNoise says an actor it calls GT13 broke into Check Point firewall management servers at 22 organisations in 17 countries, including financial firms, between mid-October and early November, using a July authentication-bypass flaw among others. It believes AI agents automated much of the work and that the campaign continues.
deck.whyItMatters: Whoever owns a firewall's management server owns the firewall; banks running Check Point should confirm the July hotfix is on every management, log and SmartEvent server and hunt for the indicators GreyNoise published.
deck.checked: Checked on GreyNoise's own write-up (opened); Check Point has not commented in what we found
deck.detailHtml: Threat-intelligence firm GreyNoise says an unattributed actor it calls GT13 broke into Check Point Security Management Servers, which control firewall policy, at at least 22 organisations in 17 countries (UK, Ireland, France, Germany, India, South Korea, Hong Kong, Australia, the US and others) between 17 Oct and 2 Nov. Victims include financial services, energy, government and transport. The actor used 99 IP addresses and a compromised relay server that held data stolen from 24 management servers, and tried exploits including CVE-2026-16232 (Check Point SmartConsole authentication bypass, patched in July), Citrix NetScaler, Ivanti and Windows NetLogon flaws. GreyNoise says it saw hands-on-keyboard activity but believes the actor used LLMs and agents for scanning, exploitation and tool-building, and that the campaign is ongoing. It is notifying victims through CERTs.

deck.headline: OpenAI says GPT-6 can design working proteins without specialised biology models
deck.summary: OpenAI says its GPT-6 models can design new proteins by reasoning and writing code, without specialised biology models. In lab tests, GPT-6.2 designs bound all five targets tried. OpenAI notes its hit rates trail specialist tools and that specialised models still filtered and selected the candidates.
deck.whyItMatters: General models are starting to replace the specialist tools in drug discovery; biotech lenders and pharma investors should watch whether design costs and timelines actually fall.
deck.detailHtml: OpenAI published a preprint, "GPT-6 as a Universal Foundation Model for Protein Biology", saying its GPT-6 family can design new protein shapes and amino-acid sequences by reasoning and writing code, without calling specialised tools such as RFdiffusion or ProteinMPNN. An internal research model matched or beat specialised models on many design tasks. In lab tests with partner Onava, at least one small protein based on GPT-6.2's 3D designs showed binding for each of five targets, and many redesigned minibinders and antibodies kept binding. OpenAI is candid about limits: its hit rates were below the original RFdiffusion study, and specialised models (Boltz-2, ESMFold2) supplied sequences and filtered candidates, so the work "does not yet establish" a fully general-model pipeline.
deck.sourcesHtml: OFFICIALOpenAI: GPT-6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities

deck.headline: Sanofi buys Insmed for $41bn to replace Dupixent's fading growth
deck.summary: Sanofi will buy Insmed for $175 a share, $41bn in cash, the biggest biopharma deal in years. It gains two approved lung drugs, Brinsupri and Arikayce, and a phase 3 programme as its blockbuster Dupixent nears the end of exclusivity. Sanofi expects the deal to add to earnings by end-2028.
deck.whyItMatters: A $41bn cash deal means a large debt raise for Sanofi; for banks it is a big underwriting and lending mandate, and a sign that big pharma will pay up for approved drugs over pipelines.
deck.detailHtml: Sanofi will pay $175 a share, $41.0bn (EUR 37.6bn) in cash and debt-financed, for US biotech Insmed, the largest biopharma acquisition in years. It gets two approved lung medicines, Brinsupri (brensocatib, the first drug for non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis) and Arikayce, plus a phase 3 inhaled therapy, TPIP. Sanofi, led by Belen Garijo, faces losing exclusivity on its blockbuster Dupixent; it expects the deal to add to earnings per share by the end of 2028 and to keep a strong credit rating. Insmed traded near $120 before Bloomberg reported talks on 19 Nov and closed at $170.15 on Tuesday.

deck.headline: US jury convicts Huawei of trade-secret theft and bank fraud, clears it of racketeering
deck.summary: A New York jury convicted Huawei on 10 of 12 counts, including conspiracy to steal trade secrets, bank fraud over its Iran business and sanctions violations, but acquitted it of racketeering. Sentencing is set for September 2027, and Huawei is expected to appeal.
deck.whyItMatters: A bank-fraud conviction for misleading lenders about Iran dealings is a reminder that sanctions screening of large corporate clients is a criminal matter, not only a compliance one.
deck.storyline: Storyline: US court cases against Chinese tech firms · day 1
deck.detailHtml: After a two-month trial in Brooklyn, a jury found Huawei guilty on 10 of 12 counts, including conspiracy to steal trade secrets from rivals, bank fraud (lying to banks about its business in Iran) and conspiracy to violate US sanctions. It was acquitted of racketeering conspiracy, which required finding it acted as a criminal enterprise. Huawei says the acquittal "vindicates" its position. Charges were first brought in 2019 after the arrest of executive Meng Wanzhou in Canada. Sentencing is planned for September 2027; Huawei's lawyer expects an appeal.

deck.headline: Free coding agent found a financial firm's access key in under six minutes
deck.summary: Security firm Jesta says an attacker used OpenCode, a free open-source coding agent, plus curl and Chrome to probe a major financial firm and find an access key, a planted decoy, in under six minutes at no cost. The bank is unnamed and the model used is unknown; one outlet reports it.
deck.whyItMatters: Attacks no longer need special malware or pentest kits; banks should assume any exposed secret in web pages, JavaScript or repos will be found within minutes, and should seed decoy keys to detect it.
deck.detailHtml: Tel Aviv security startup Jesta told The Register that on 16 Nov someone in Bucharest pointed OpenCode, a free open-source coding agent that works with 200+ model providers, at a major financial-services customer's website. Using only the agent, the Mac's built-in curl and Chrome, it tried several ways in and found an access key (a planted decoy) in under six minutes, at no cost to the operator. Jesta identified the agent from its web-fetch tool's signature; it does not know which model was used. "Nothing in OpenCode was built for hacking," its CTO said, but nothing stops it being pointed at someone else's site.
deck.sourcesHtml: REPORTINGThe Register: An AI coding agent, a browser, and a Mac tool found a financial firm's access key in under 6 minutes

deck.headline: Radware and Rackspace breaches expose customers' cloud keys and Kubernetes secrets
deck.summary: Radware says an internal Cloud WAF API left open without authentication was accessed on 19 Nov, exposing customer contacts and some customers' S3, Azure and SFTP log-export keys. Rackspace is shutting its Spot Kubernetes platform on 8 Dec after attackers read customer cluster secrets.
deck.whyItMatters: The security vendors in a bank's stack hold keys to its storage; ask every WAF, DDoS and cloud provider which of your credentials they keep, and rotate Radware log-export keys now if you use Cloud WAF.
deck.storyline: Storyline: attacks through software and vendors · day 10
deck.detailHtml: Radware, which protects 12,500 enterprises and carriers, says an unauthorised party on 19 Nov accessed an internal Cloud WAF management API that was reachable from the internet without authentication. Exposed: customer contact details and, for some, the credentials used to export logs to their own AWS S3, Azure Blob or SFTP storage. It detected the breach ten hours later and tells AppSec customers to rotate those keys; some have seen AWS alerts from an unfamiliar IP. Separately, Rackspace is shutting down Rackspace Spot on 8 Dec after attackers used stolen credentials on 17 Nov to create pods in customer Kubernetes clusters and read cluster secrets.
deck.sourcesHtml: REPORTINGBleepingComputer: Radware discloses breach exposing customer cloud access keys · BleepingComputer: Rackspace shuts down Spot cloud platform after security breach

deck.headline: Microsoft declares 'Code Red' after its worst-ever Exchange Online outage
deck.summary: Microsoft has declared an internal 'Code Red' after the nearly 24-hour Exchange Online and Microsoft 365 outage of 12-13 Nov, memos reported by Reuters show. It aims to fix worldwide incidents within an hour using AI agents; one urgent fix took five to six days to reach every server.
deck.whyItMatters: Banks running email, trading chat and Copilot on one provider should test how they work through a full-day outage; Microsoft itself says it cannot yet push an urgent fix worldwide in an hour.
deck.storyline: Storyline: when one cloud fails · day 8
deck.detailHtml: Internal memos reported by Reuters show Microsoft has declared a "Code Red", its highest internal priority, after the nearly 24-hour outage of Exchange Online, Outlook, Teams and Copilot on 12-13 Nov that hit governments, trading firms and airlines. Microsoft 365 Core president Jason Henderson called it the most customer-affecting incident in Exchange Online's history and admitted past work "had not been enough". Another memo describes a "fog of war": responders exchanged over 11,000 messages in 11 Teams chats. The plan covers load shedding, geographic traffic partitioning and faster recovery, with a goal of fixing worldwide incidents within an hour; one urgent production fix took five to six days to reach every server.

deck.headline: South Korea's draft law hands won stablecoins to bank-led groups
deck.summary: South Korea's FSC has drafted a law under which bank-majority groups would issue won stablecoins, with 100% reserves, face-value redemption and at least 5bn won of capital. Shareholders in crypto exchanges would be capped at 20%, and the 2017 ban on domestic coin offerings would end.
deck.whyItMatters: Another major economy is putting stablecoins inside the banking system rather than beside it; Korean banks become the gatekeepers, and foreign issuers face a bank-partnered route.
deck.detailHtml: South Korea's Financial Services Commission published a draft bill on Tuesday under which won-denominated stablecoins could at first be issued only by groups in which banks collectively own more than half, though a fintech or tech firm could be the largest single shareholder. Issuers would need FSC authorisation, at least 5bn won (about $3.7m) of capital, 100% reserves and redemption at face value without delay. Crypto exchanges would need dealing, brokerage and custody licences, and any shareholder would be capped at 20% (34% with approval). The bill would also lift the 2017 ban on domestic coin offerings. It settles a long fight: the central bank wanted banks in control; the FSC had favoured non-banks too. A Korean report says the won-stablecoin rollout may slip to 2028.
deck.sourcesHtml: REPORTINGCointelegraph: South Korea proposes bank-led stablecoins, 20% cap on crypto exchange stakes

deck.headline: Dell lifts its AI server forecast to $78bn and adds a $25bn buyback
deck.summary: Dell raised its forecasts for the third time this year: fiscal 2027 revenue of $202bn and AI server revenue of $78bn, up from $74bn. It added a $25bn buyback, and shares rose about 5% after hours. HP also beat revenue forecasts.
deck.whyItMatters: Enterprise AI hardware spending is still rising even as AI stocks wobble; for banks, the data-centre capex cycle that backs much AI credit has not turned yet.
deck.storyline: Storyline: building AI's power and data centres · day 31
deck.detailHtml: Dell raised its annual forecasts for the third time this year after a record quarter. It now expects fiscal 2027 revenue of $202bn (from $192bn; analysts expected $194.5bn), AI-optimised server revenue of $78bn (from $74bn) and adjusted EPS of $29.68 (from $25.50). The board approved another $25bn share buyback and shares rose about 5% after hours, recovering part of a 12% fall in Tuesday's session. Its PC business grew more slowly. Rival HP reported quarterly revenue of $16bn, above the $15.4bn expected.

deck.headline: A 27B ternary model in 5.9GB nearly matches its full-size base on coding agents
deck.summary: PrismML's Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B stores weights as one of three values and fits in 5.9GB, yet scores 75.6 on SWE-bench Verified against 80.6 for its full-size Qwen base. It runs at 204 tokens a second on a consumer RTX 4090. The benchmarks are the company's own.
deck.whyItMatters: A near-frontier coding agent that fits on a laptop GPU makes private, on-premises agents realistic for code and documents that cannot leave a bank; the scores are the company's own.
deck.storyline: Storyline: new kinds of AI models · day 12
deck.detailHtml: PrismML released Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B, which stores each weight as one of three values and keeps Qwen3.8 27B's abilities in a 5.9GB file. On its own benchmarks it scores 75.6 on SWE-bench Verified (full-precision base 80.6; its previous version 60.8), 90.5 on AppWorld (base 93.2) and 60.1 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (base 70.8). It runs at 291 tokens/s on one Nvidia H100 and 204 on a consumer RTX 4090. The update targets long chains of tool calls and fixes over-thinking loops in version 2. GGUF weights are on Hugging Face; the launch drew 302 points on Hacker News.

deck.headline: Utah drops criminal charges after Kalshi leaves the state
deck.summary: Kalshi halted trading in Utah for its 177,000 users after losing court bids against the state's gambling enforcement, and a day later Utah moved to drop criminal charges against the company and its founders. The CFTC replaced 17 prediction-market waivers with one reporting rule.
deck.whyItMatters: State gambling law is winning the first rounds against federally regulated event contracts; banks and brokers looking at prediction-market partnerships face state-by-state risk.
deck.storyline: Storyline: prediction markets and their rules · day 8
deck.detailHtml: Kalshi paused operations in Utah on 23 Nov after losing court fights, including a federal appeals bid, to stop the state enforcing its gambling laws; a CFTC emergency motion arguing federal jurisdiction has not been granted. "This is an unfortunate outcome for the more than 177,000 Utahns who use Kalshi," its spokesperson said. A day later Utah's attorney general moved to drop criminal charges against the company and its co-founders. A New York judge had declined on 23 Nov to block Kalshi there for now. The CFTC also adopted a single permanent reporting rule for prediction markets in place of 17 separate waivers.
deck.sourcesHtml: REPORTINGArs Technica: Kalshi makes 'difficult decision' to halt Utah trading after losing court fights · The Hill: Utah moves to dismiss criminal case against Kalshi · Cointelegraph: CFTC sets new prediction market rules as more firms seek US entry

deck.headline: Trump calls a Huang pardon 'an option' as Congress prepares its questions
deck.summary: Trump says pardoning Jensen Huang is 'an option' he doesn't expect to need, and the attorney general won't say whether the DOJ or FBI investigated him. Megaspeed is now on the Entity List. Huang faces House committees on 1 Dec, and Nvidia shares fell 5.9% on Tuesday.
deck.whyItMatters: Talk of a pardon before any charge keeps the legal and governance risk around Nvidia open; banks with Nvidia exposure should watch the 1 Dec interview and any DOJ statement.
deck.update: Pressure moves to Washington: Trump says a pardon for Huang is 'an option' he doesn't expect to need, the attorney general won't say whether DOJ or the FBI investigated him, Megaspeed is now on the Entity List, and Nvidia shares give back 5.9%.
deck.detailHtml: President Trump told the New York Post that pardoning Jensen Huang is "always an option" but he doesn't think it will be necessary. Attorney General Todd Blanche called Nvidia a "good corporate citizen" but, asked repeatedly whether the DOJ or FBI had investigated Huang, said: "I don't know what you're talking about." The Commerce Department has now added Megaspeed, the Singapore cloud firm linked to Alice Huang, and its subsidiaries to the Entity List; trade experts say the rule leaves out a clause such listings usually include. Hakeem Jeffries called the reinstatement "indefensible"; Republican Don Bacon called it "inexplicable". Huang is due to face House committees in a recorded interview on 1 Dec and the Senate Banking Committee later. Nvidia fell 5.9% to $155.38.
deck.sourcesHtml: REPORTINGTechCrunch: Trump reportedly says pardoning Jensen Huang is 'an option' · BBC: US attorney general dodges questions about Nvidia investigation · SiliconANGLE: Congress scrutinizes Jensen Huang's return as Megaspeed restrictions raise questions

alsoToday.headline: New benchmark: top AI agents fail over a third of everyday tasks
alsoToday.summary: ShellBench, built from more than 10 million anonymised real-world agent interactions by the OpenClaw Foundation, Parsewave, Hugging Face, Red Hat and UC Berkeley, tests the everyday errands people hand to personal agents. Even the most advanced models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta failed more than a third of tasks, and 15.7% of all attempts broke at least one safety requirement.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: Banks deciding how far to let customers' agents act on accounts have new evidence that agents still make costly mistakes a third of the time.

alsoToday.headline: Hong Kong will make banks register with the SFC before holding clients' crypto
alsoToday.summary: Under a bill gazetted by the Hong Kong government, banks and stored-value facility operators supervised by the HKMA would need an additional registration with the Securities and Futures Commission to safeguard, trade, advise on or manage virtual assets for customers; independent custodians would need an SFC licence.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: Banks in Hong Kong wanting to hold clients' crypto now face a dual-regulator route, which raises the bar for custody offerings.
alsoToday.detailHtml: Under a bill gazetted by the Hong Kong government, banks and stored-value facility operators supervised by the HKMA would need an additional registration with the Securities and Futures Commission to safeguard, trade, advise on or manage virtual assets for customers; independent custodians would need an SFC licence. The HKMA expects institutions planning digital-asset custody to talk to it in advance and meet its standards on segregating customer assets and safeguarding private keys. Timing depends on the legislation.

alsoToday.headline: US seeks $1.1bn of stolen Binance USDC, with Circle reissuing the tokens
alsoToday.summary: The Justice Department filed a civil forfeiture complaint in Washington on 23 Nov targeting more than $1.1bn of frozen USDC stolen in Binance's October hack, reported at about $6bn. Because prosecutors cannot reach the attackers' private keys, Circle has agreed to issue replacement USDC to the government if a court approves forfeiture, while the stolen tokens stay frozen.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: Issuer-controlled stablecoins can be frozen and reissued by court order, which matters for any bank that holds or settles in them, both as protection and as a legal exposure.

alsoToday.headline: Cyberattack takes down Colorado's digital ID app and steals data on 150,000
alsoToday.summary: Colorado's Office of Information Technology says hackers breached the myColorado app, which 2.1 million residents use for digital ID, document storage and state services, on the evening of 18 Nov. The app remains offline, and data tied to nearly 150,000 people was likely stolen; the state has not said what data.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: State digital IDs are becoming identity-verification inputs for bank onboarding; a breach of one is a fraud risk for KYC teams.

alsoToday.headline: Anthropic study: AI brings fewer hires rather than layoffs at 58 companies
alsoToday.summary: Anthropic's economics team interviewed people at 58 companies that use Claude. They described few layoffs but reduced hiring, and said the most valuable uses of AI often came from reorganising roles and workplaces around it rather than bolting it onto existing jobs.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: The first labour effect is on entry-level hiring, not on existing staff; graduate and analyst intakes are where banks will see it first.

alsoToday.headline: Uber and Nuro start driverless tests of Lucid robotaxis in the Bay Area
alsoToday.summary: Uber and Nuro have started testing Lucid Gravity SUVs with no one in the driver's seat on public streets in the San Francisco Bay Area, ahead of a commercial robotaxi launch planned for 2027. alsoToday.headline: Court reinstates Senegal as Africa Cup of Nations champions, ten months on
alsoToday.summary: The Court of Arbitration for Sport ruled that Senegal are the winners of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations, overturning the decision that stripped them of the title they won on the pitch in January.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: Ten months after the final, the title is still in court, which shows how far sports governance disputes now run through lawyers.
alsoToday.detailHtml: The Court of Arbitration for Sport ruled that Senegal are the winners of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations, overturning the decision that stripped them of the title they won on the pitch in January. With the final against hosts Morocco goalless in stoppage time, Senegal had left the field in protest at a penalty awarded against them, delaying the match in Rabat by more than 15 minutes. Morocco says it will take further legal action.
